Minutes of the 108th Meeting of the Chamber of Deputies, Solem Non-Deliberative Morning Session, 4th Ordinary Legislative Session, 55th Legislature, on May 14, 2018.

Presiding Officers:
Alberto Fraga, Izalci Lucas, in accordance with Article 18, §2, of the Internal Regulation.

Minutes of the 108th (eighty-eighth) Meeting of the Chamber of Deputies, Solem Non-Deliberative Morning Session, 4th Ordinary Legislative Session, 55th Legislature, on May 14, 2018. At 10:17 a.m., Mr. Alberto Fraga, presiding in accordance with Article 18, §2, of the Internal Regulation, opened the session and waived the reading of the minutes from the previous meeting. The President requested a moment of silence in memory of the 4th Secretary of the Chamber of Deputies, Mr. Rômulo Gouveia. He then announced that the session would honor the Military Police of the Federal District (PMDF), paid tribute accordingly, and invited to the presidium Mr. Izalci Lucas, author of the request; Colonel William Delano Marques de Araújo, Commander of the Community Police and Human Rights Center, representing Colonel Marcos Antônio Nunes de Oliveira, General Commander of PMDF; Colonel Arnaldo da Costa Farias Filho, from the II Metropolitan Regional Command, representing Colonel Fábio Aracaqui de Sousa Lima, Deputy Commander of PMDF; Colonel Edgar Cesar Rojas, from the II Western Regional Command, representing Colonel Ricardo Yamazaki Santiago, Chief of Staff of PMDF; and Colonel Marcylon Back da Silva, Chief of the Operational Department of PMDF. The President invited everyone to listen to the National Anthem and the Song of the Military Police of the Federal District, performed by the Military Police Band of the Federal District, under the direction of Maestro Josael Albertino Moreira, General Music Director of PMDF Band. He then invited everyone to listen to “The History of PMDF,” told by teacher and storyteller Nyedja Gennari. After the institutional video, the President delivered the speech of Mr. Rodrigo Maia, President of the Chamber of Deputies, and granted the floor to Mr. Izalci Lucas, author of the request. During his speech, he presented a certificate of honor to merit to Mr. First Lieutenant Herison de Oliveira Bezerra; Sergeant Cleônio Rodrigues de Sousa; and First Sergeant Arizomar Pereira Gonçalves. In accordance with Article 18, §2, of the Internal Regulation, Mr. Izalci Lucas assumed the presidency and granted the floor to Mr. Alberto Fraga, author of the request. During his speech, he presented a certificate of honor to merit to Major Graziela Guedes Salgado; Sergeant Heitor Theodoro da Silva; Third Sergeant Marcelo Brito Magalhães; and Samantha Moreira da Costa Santos, widow of Corporal Luciano Pereira dos Santos. The President then granted the floor to members of the presidium, William Delano Marques de Araújo; Arnaldo da Costa Farias Filho; and Marcylon Back da Silva. The President noted the presence of guests, reiterated the tributes, thanked everyone for their attendance, and at 11:32 a.m., adjourned the session.

Rodrigo Maia
President

COMPLEMENTARY LAW No. 499, of 2018
(From the Federal Senate)
PLS No. 350/2015
OFÍCIO nº 497/18 (SF)
Provides for competition defense within the scope of financial institutions and other institutions subject to supervision or surveillance by the Central Bank of Brazil and for cooperation and sharing of competences between the Central Bank of Brazil and the Administrative Council for Economic Defense (Cade) in competition matters, and repeals Article 18, §2, of Law No. 4,595, of December 31, 1964.
DISPOSITION:
ATTACH TO PLP-265/2007.
CONSIDERATION:
Proposition Subject to Plenary Consideration
The National Congress decrees:
CHAPTER I
PRELIMINARY PROVISIONS
Article 1. This Complementary Law provides for competition defense within the scope of financial institutions and other institutions subject to supervision or surveillance by the Central Bank of Brazil and for cooperation and sharing of competences between the Central Bank of Brazil and the Administrative Council for Economic Defense (Cade) in competition matters.
Article 2º O. The Central Bank of Brazil and Cade, within their respective spheres of competence, shall coordinate their activities to ensure the fulfillment of their duties with greater efficiency and lower cost to the regulated entities.
Sole Paragraph. The Central Bank of Brazil and Cade shall maintain a permanent forum for communication, including through a technical cooperation agreement, to comply with this Complementary Law.
CHAPTER II
CONCENTRATION ACTS
Article 3. It is the responsibility of the Central Bank of Brazil and Cade to examine concentration acts between financial institutions.
§ 1. Petitions regarding concentration acts shall be submitted by the interested parties to the Central Bank of Brazil and Cade, in accordance with the deadlines and conditions established in regulations to be jointly issued by the autonomous agencies.
§ 2. The examination of the petitions referred to in § 1 shall be conducted in each agency through its own procedures and regulations.
§ 3. In conducting the examination of concentration acts, the Central Bank of Brazil and Cade shall share information and studies regarding the operation, subject to legal confidentiality, with a view to converging technical parameters, in accordance with the conditions established in the joint regulation referred to in § 1.
§ 4. Except for the situation provided for in Article 4, the effectiveness of concentration acts involving financial institutions is conditioned on the authorization of both agencies, in accordance with the deadlines and conditions established in the joint regulation referred to in § 1.
May 2018
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES
Tuesday 15 27

**Conditions as stipulated in the joint regulation referred to in § 1.**

**§ 5** Without prejudice to the competence of CADE, in accordance with the applicable legislation, the Central Bank of Brazil may conclude concentration control agreements with interested parties.

**§ 6º O** The agreement provided for in § 5 may be concluded jointly by the Central Bank of Brazil and CADE, as stipulated in the joint regulation referred to in § 1.

**Art. 4º O** The Central Bank of Brazil may unilaterally approve concentration acts involving financial institutions whenever prudential aspects indicate significant and imminent risks to the solidity and stability of the National Financial System.

**§ 1** An operation with prudential aspects is one that, in the judgment of the Central Bank of Brazil:

I – involves a risk to the solidity of a financial institution or a segment of the National Financial System;

II – compromises the maintenance of the stability of the National Financial System and the prevention of systemic crisis;

III – impairs the effectiveness of a resolution regime applied to a financial institution;

IV – impairs the effectiveness of measures necessary to mitigate the need for application of a resolution regime;

V – impairs the effectiveness of measures necessary to reverse the trajectory of loss of solidity of a financial institution or a segment of the National Financial System with a business model identified as inconsistent, vulnerable, or unviable.

**§ 2** Upon approval of a concentration act by the Central Bank of Brazil, as provided in the preceding paragraph, the Central Bank of Brazil shall notify CADE of its decision within one (1) business day, indicating the grounds for its decision and stating whether the prudential aspects cover the entire operation or only specific relevant markets.

**§ 3** In the case of § 2, CADE shall approve the operation without restrictions, using the grounds of the Central Bank of Brazil's decision as a basis for recognizing economic efficiency and development, in accordance with Article 88, § 6, item I, subitem c, of Law No. 12,529 of November 30, 2011.

**§ 4** The CADE's analysis, as provided in § 3, does not prevent the immediate implementation of the concentration act, and the provisions of Article 88, § 3, of Law No. 12,259 of November 30, 2011, do not apply.

**§ 5** In addition to notification by the Central Bank of Brazil, as provided in § 2, the parties shall notify CADE, in accordance with Article 53 of Law No. 12,529 of November 30, 2011, under penalty of imposition of a monetary fine, with a value not less than R$ 60,000.00 (sixty thousand reais) nor exceeding R$ 60,000,000.00 (sixty million reais), without prejudice to the initiation of an administrative proceeding, in accordance with Article 69 of Law No. 12,529 of November 30, 2011.

**CHAPTER III**

**ON THE CONTROL OF BEHAVIORS INVOLVING INSTITUTIONS UNDER THE SUPERVISION OR SURVEILLANCE OF THE CENTRAL BANK OF BRAZIL**

**Art. 5º O** The Central Bank of Brazil and CADE shall independently and autonomously decide on the existence of infringements involving institutions under the supervision or surveillance of the Central Bank of Brazil and shall apply the penalties provided by law, in accordance with the competences established in the applicable legislation, subject to the provisions of Article 6 of this Complementary Law.

**Single Paragraph** In exercising the powers provided for in the preceding paragraph:

I – the Central Bank of Brazil shall apply the provisions of Law No. 13,506 of November 13, 2017, in cases of non-compliance with legal and regulatory norms whose compliance falls within its supervisory scope;

II – CADE shall apply the provisions of Law No. 12,529 of November 30, 2011, in cases of economic order infringements.

COMPLEMENTARY LAW No. 502, of 2018
(Mr. Junji Abe)
Adds a provision to Complementary Law No. 123, of December 14, 2006, to establish a readjustment of the annual gross revenue limit for the option of the Special Regime of the Individual Microentrepreneur (MEI), as specified.

DISPOSITION:
ATTACH TO PLP-327/2016.

CONSIDERATION:
Proposal Subject to Plenary Consideration
The National Congress decrees:

Article 1. This Law amends Complementary Law No. 123, of December 14, 2006, to establish a criterion for readjusting the gross revenue ceiling for the Individual Microentrepreneur (MEI).

Article 2. Add § 26 to Article 18-A of Complementary Law No. 123, of December 14, 2006, as follows:

"Article 18-A .....................................................................................
.....................................................................................................
§ 26. The ceiling provided for in § 1 of this Article shall be readjusted in January of each year
in accordance with the variation of the National Consumer Price Index (INPC), or any other index
that may replace it, as verified in the previous year." (NR)

Article 3. This Complementary Law shall enter into force on the date of its publication.

JUSTIFICATION
Honorable Colleagues, we believe that this matter deserves due attention, as it seems appropriate to create a mechanism to readjust the limits of the Special Regime of the Individual Microentrepreneur (MEI), which has proven to be extremely productive for integrating and formalizing millions of small businesses that were previously operating outside the law, prevented from progressing and benefiting from the formal economy.

In fact, the MEI is an opportunity for those who work for themselves to gain rights and formalize a small business without costs or bureaucracy. However, we know that an MEI entrepreneur who experiences an increase in revenue above the annual limit of R$ 81,000.00, as a result of the growth of his business, begins to face differentiated taxation.

The problem is that many small businesses classified as MEI have their costs linked to the minimum wage due to legal requirements. Therefore, an increase in revenue that does not exceed the ceiling may result in a higher tax burden for these entrepreneurs.
30 Tuesday 15
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES
May 2018

Overcoming this cost increase should not be considered as a de-characterization of the status of individual micro-entrepreneur. Thus, we are proposing that the MEI (Micro and Small Entrepreneur Individual) classification limit be readjusted by the National Consumer Price Index - INPC of the previous year, one of the indicators for setting the minimum wage.

We are clear about the merit of this initiative, which is why we request the support of the Noble Peers for the approval of this proposal.

Chamber of Sessions, on May 02, 2018.

COMPLEMENTARY LAW PROJECT No. 503, OF 2018
(From Mr. Danilo Cabral)
Provides for the alienation of public companies' assets and assets in the last year of an elected term.
DISPACH:
TO THE COMMITTEES OF:
FINANCE AND TAXATION (MERIT AND ART. 54, RICD) AND
CONSTITUTION AND JUSTICE AND CITIZENSHIP (ART. 54 RICD)
CONSIDERATION:
Proposal Subject to Plenary Consideration
The National Congress decrees:
Art. 1 Complementary Law No. 101, of May 4, 2000 (Fiscal Responsibility Law), is hereby amended by adding Article 44-A, which reads as follows:
"Art. 44-A. The alienation of assets and assets that are part of the permanent patrimony of public companies or state-owned mixed companies, as well as the total or partial transfer of corporate control or operations under its responsibility, is prohibited in the last year of the term of office of the President, Governor, or Municipal Mayor."
Art. This complementary law shall enter into force on the date of its publication.
JUSTIFICATION
This Complementary Law Project reprises and deepens the intention that guided the elaboration of the very Fiscal Responsibility Law - LRF that it seeks to amend. It is, after all, now, as it was in 2000 when it was promulgated, aimed at establishing criteria and limits to prevent the state management from becoming an instrument of public patrimony depletion.
It is no coincidence, indeed, that the Fiscal Responsibility Law contains a specific chapter dedicated to patrimonial management (Chapter VIII) and, within it, a section dedicated to the preservation of public patrimony (Section II). Both the chapter and the section indicate that the legislator's concern went beyond the protection of the administration's cash flow, aiming at preserving the State's patrimonial stock.
In fact, ultimately, this second concern should be decisive, as it is in this area that the greatest depredations, the most demeaning expropriations of assets belonging to the Brazilian people can occur.
In this sense, it is not an exaggeration to argue that the PLP not only reprises but also deepens the intention of the Law. The passage of time has only reinforced the perception that, in 2000, culminating a process that spanned the 1990s, the legislator's attention was overly focused on expenditure control, or, at best, on budget execution.
32 Tuesday 15
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES
May 2018

**Translation:**

The guarantee of short and medium-term balance between revenues and expenses is crucial when the well-being of the population is intimately linked to the preservation of the state's patrimonial capacity to fulfill its legitimate aspirations for quality public services. This aspect of the issue has thus been placed in a partially secondary plane; deepening the intentionality of the Law means, therefore, giving it the appropriate prominence in the legal order, as this proposal aims to do.

Certainly, none of this implies the irrelevancy of the effort to achieve the state's fiscal balance. On the contrary, when fiscal balance is not simply understood as reducing social expenses, which, surprisingly, sometimes happens, it becomes a condition for good governance and investment in improved living conditions for the population. Here, it is not argued for eliminating the ability to manage public property when circumstances demand it. There is no reason to assume that the state should forever remain in the areas of action chosen in the past, due to purposes that may be obsolete. The intention is to prevent hasty measures, against the clock, to secure cash resources for immediate purposes or, worse, to please sectors that might favor those in office in their eventual desire to remain in power.

Article 42 of the LRF (Law of Fiscal Responsibility) prevents the management, at the end of the term, from incurring an obligation for expenses that cannot be fully met during the term (an obligation that, obviously, may involve squandering, but it can also represent a relevant investment for the population). The Law should, therefore, be even more concerned with the possibility that the same management, just before the end of the term, disposes of property hardily produced by the country, often resulting from the effort of generations.

It is noteworthy that the LRF demonstrates a special concern with measures taken in the last year of the terms of office of those in power. This is the case, for instance, with the restriction on increasing expenditure on personnel (Article 21, § unique) and the prohibition of credit operations by anticipation of revenue (Article 38, IV, b). In this regard, it aligns with Law No. 9,504 of September 30, 1997 (Electoral Law), which dedicates a chapter to prohibited conduct for public servants during election campaigns. In both cases, the norms reflect the understanding that the last year of the terms of office is particularly susceptible to governmental initiatives driven by the interests of groups or sectors with which the rulers have a privileged relationship, to the detriment of general public interests.

It is precisely because this Complementary Law Project does not conflict with the concerns that led to the approval of the Law of Fiscal Responsibility, but rather extends and deepens them, that we count on its approval, in the short term, by the members of the House.

Chamber of Sessions, May 2, 2018.

Danilo Cabral
PSB/PE
May 2018

COMPLEMENTARY BILL NO. 506, OF 2018
(From Mr. Carlos Henrique Gaguim)
Amends Complementary Law No. 105, of January 10, 2001, to provide that the publication and sharing of information relating to credit operations concluded with entities of the Federation does not constitute a breach of the banking secrecy duty.
DISPOSITION:
ATTACH TO PLP-327/2013.
CONSIDERATION:
Proposal subject to plenary consideration
The National Congress decrees:
Article 1. This Complementary Law concerns the publication and sharing of information relating to credit operations concluded by financial institutions with entities of the Federation.
Article 2º O The article 1st of Complementary Law No. 105, of January 10, 2001, is replaced by the following:
"Article 1. ..........................................................................................
.....................................................................................................
§3. ..............................................................................................
....................................................................................................
VII - Sharing with control bodies and the publication of any information relating to credit operations concluded by financial institutions with legal entities of public law.
..................................................................................................".
Article 3. Financial institutions shall publish on their websites copies of contracts that facilitate credit operations concluded with legal entities of public law.
Article 4. This Complementary Law enters into force on the date of its official publication.
JUSTIFICATION
The protection of banking secrecy is a consequence of the fundamental guarantees of privacy and intimacy, ensured by the 1988 Constitution. From them, the legal mandate, provided for in Complementary Law No. 105, of January 10, 2000, arises that information relating to operations concluded by financial institutions shall not be disclosed.
36 Tuesday 15
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES
May 2018

It happens that the protection of privacy and intimacy may give way to other interests,
particularly the preservation of other fundamental guarantees and clauses.
When it comes to credit operations contracted by legal entities of public law, it seems to us that
the republican principle prevails, which recommends maximum transparency regarding measures that
involve the indebtedness of the Public Administration. It does not even make sense to talk about
privacy or intimacy of entities of the Federation or their public autonomous bodies and foundations.
For these reasons, we present this complementary bill, which amends the legislation on bank secrecy
to provide that the duty of secrecy imposed on financial institutions does not apply to operations
they enter into with legal entities of public law.
We count on the support of our Colleagues to debate and approve this proposal.
Chamber of Sessions, May 9, 2018.

**Article 1**

This Complementary Law amends Complementary Law No. 116 of July 31, 2003, as amended by Complementary Law No. 157 of December 29, 2016, which provides for the Tax on Services of Any Nature, of municipal and Federal District competence, and establishes other provisions.

**Article 2**

Complementary Law No. 116 of July 31, 2003, is hereby amended to include the following legal provisions:

"Article 3a. The following natural and legal persons shall be considered service users described in subparagraph XXIII of Article 3 of this Complementary Law:

I. In the case of services described in items 4.22 and 4.23 of the service list annexed to this Complementary Law, the user/beneficiary, a natural person linked to the operator through a health plan contract and/or individual or family agreement, or a collective business or adhere collective agreement.

II. In the case of services described in item 5.09 of the service list annexed to this Complementary Law, the natural or legal person who contracts a medical and veterinary care plan."

"Article 3b. The following natural and legal persons shall be considered service users described in subparagraph XXIV of Article 3 of this Complementary Law:

I. In the case of fund management services, the service user is the quota holder.

II. In the case of consortium management services, the service user is the consortium member.

III. In the case of portfolio customer management, pre-dated check management, and similar services, the service user shall be the management entity itself."

"Article 3c. In the case of services described in subparagraph XXV of Article 3 of this Complementary Law, the user's domicile shall be:

I. In the case of commercial lease (leasing) services, the service user is the lessee.

II. In the case of franchise (franchising) services, the service user is the franchisee.

III. In the case of factoring (faturization) services, the service user is the factored entity."

**Article 3**

This Law shall enter into force on the date of its publication, repealing any contrary provisions.

**Justification**

The proposed Complementary Law presented here aims to clarify ambiguities arising from the amendment to Complementary Law No. 116/2003 by Complementary Law No. 157/2016 regarding...
38 Tuesday 15
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES
May 2018

The place of service provision and subsequent collection of the Service Tax - ISS.
With the amendment brought about by LC 157/2016, in LC 116/2003, the collection of ISS for credit and debit card services, leasing, health plans, merchant leasing (leasing), franchising, and factoring, is now due in the municipality of the service recipient's domicile, rather than the municipality where the establishments are headquartered.
As a result, some services that have undergone changes regarding the place of ISS payment, require identifying the legal entities capable of receiving them, as this municipality will be the one holding the collected ISS.
Accordingly, the approval of this Complementary Law Project is necessary to determine who the service recipients are for certain activities, thus eliminating any discrepancies in municipal legislation that could lead to double taxation of the said tribute.
For instance, we refer to the merchant leasing (leasing) activity, one of the activities affected by the change in LC 157/2016. Previously, when an individual purchased a good in a specific city through the leasing modality, the ISS was due to the municipality where the lessor's headquarters were located. Now, with the amendment brought about by LC 157/2016, in LC 116/2003, the tax will be collected by the municipal entity where the lessee resides.
The new ISS Law requires significant changes and adjustments in the respective laws of the municipalities. Therefore, the municipal administrator must stay vigilant regarding these new changes and adapt the Municipal Tax Code to accommodate the alterations brought about by LC 116/2003.
However, due to the news circulating, the "new" taxpayers are unsure of whom to pay, and in order to prevent distortions regarding who should collect the ISS in the cases addressed here, the approval of this Complementary Law is necessary.
Indeed, taxpayers affected by the change in LC 116/2003 have filed actions at the STF (Supreme Court), one of the arguments being to define who is the recipient of the services impacted by this amended Complementary Law.
It is important to emphasize the urgency and necessity of approving this law project, given that in thousands of municipalities, the decline in revenues has been increasing year by year, affecting essential services to the population in many places.
And, given the uncertainty regarding which municipal entity the taxpayers should pay the ISS under the new legislation, the swift approval of this law project is indispensable for Brazilian municipalities to benefit from these funds.

Chamber of Commissions, May 8, 2018.

HILDO ROCHA
FEDERAL DEPUTY
May 2018

Violent deaths per 100,000 inhabitants,1 a figure that rose to 28.6 in 2015 and jumped to 29.7 in 2016.2 The country also ranks as the 7th most violent in Latin America. There are no signs of improvement on the horizon.

Reducing lethal violence requires, in addition to effective prevention and repression policies, strengthening homicide investigation. As pointed out by the research "Where Does Impunity Live?" by the Institute for Peace and Society3, despite targeted investments in some capitals to create specialized homicide delegations and improve forensic bodies, studies show weak performance by Brazilian police in solving homicides. In some states, the Public Ministry charges less than 15% of violent deaths due to weaknesses in evidence, forensic structure deficits, and excessive delays in conducting police inquiries, among other factors.

According to the mentioned research, most violent deaths solved in the country involve crimes in domestic contexts between couples or that preceded flagrant arrests, generally involving close and easier-to-investigate individuals. Many cases involving organized crime end up stalled in delegations or proceed for years between state police and the Public Ministry without resolution, fueling impunity and hindering the design of targeted public policies. No wonder Brazilian states that achieved the best rates of reduction in their lethal violence indices were those that implemented qualified prevention projects and physical, technological, scientific, and methodological restructuring of their specialized police units in homicide investigation. The more information about the phenomenon, authors, and victims of intentional homicide, the better the subsidies for programs aimed at its containment.

Based on this study, we present this proposal with the objective of creating a National Homicide Clarification Indicator that allows safely measuring the performance of criminal investigations in each federal unit.

This indicator aims to demonstrate what proportion of homicide investigations in federal units leads to a criminal action, what the outcome of this action is, and what existing structure promotes the investigation of lethal crimes.

This will make it possible to provide transparency and enable social control over the allocation of material and human resources to public security, allowing us to assess whether public managers are prioritizing the investigation of crimes that cause the most suffering to society or if they are allocating existing resources to meet other demands.

The creation of the National Homicide Clarification Indicator will enable the setting of goals and the consolidation of good practices focused on investigation and criminal prosecution, measure the advances achieved in each federal unit, and foster the exchange of successful experiences among police, experts, and prosecutors, allowing for a joint strategic planning of the bodies that make up the security and justice system.

As highlighted by the Institute for Peace and Society study: homicide investigation and processing by institutions that make up the criminal justice and security system in Brazil is ineffective and inefficient. In 2012, the National Public Ministry Council, in monitoring work of Meta 2 of the National Strategy for Justice and Public Security, pointed to very low rates of homicide clarification in Brazilian states. In São Paulo, the Sou da Paz Institute published an October 2017 survey on a representative sample of dolus homicides inquiries, of which 34% resulted in criminal complaints and only 5% reached trial.
As the study indicates, it is impossible to compare the results of the investigative systems of the states, as there is no national indicator that allows for uniform data collection. Furthermore, the low homicide clarification rates and excessive delays in processing cases are attributed to the predominance of public investments in overt policing, the scarcity of civil and technical-scientific police officers, and poor working conditions, which lead to the inadequacy of key technical-pericial procedures, such as the delimitation, isolation, and preservation of crime scenes. In most cases, homicide inquiries rely primarily on witness indications and have a cartular character. The peritia, fundamental for the production of technical evidence, tends to confirm the delictive materiality but not the authorship, shedding light on "what happened, but not who killed." Adding to these deficiencies the limited institutional articulation between the bodies that make up the criminal justice system, the low quality of the criminal procedure instruction in homicide cases is among the drivers of impunity in Brazil.
The creation of a National Homicide Clarification Indicator, composed of data related to the entire investigation and trial process of these crimes, as well as the structure provided for the exercise of these activities, will allow assessing how and in what way each ruler deals with this situation, enabling social control over the prioritization given to homicide inquiries.

Moreover, undeniably, we are in a period of extensive and deep judicialization in all aspects of society, particularly regarding political issues.
Recently, we have seen an innumerable number of decisions in specific constitutional review actions that have generated turbulent situations of immense reach.
A significant factor in constitutional review actions are, in particular, the effects of preliminary injunctions, if granted, as they resemble almost the entirety of the own merits effects.
Thus, as already mentioned, the effects of preliminary injunctions resemble the merits, therefore with complex reach, which obviously have effects beyond the mere petitioner.

Thus, it becomes necessary to enable the author, once the precautionary request is presented,
provided that for duly justified reasons within the legal framework, and in the face of a loss of material and procedural interest in the urgency measure, to voluntarily withdraw the action.
Such a measure, in our opinion, is extremely necessary as it allows the author of the action to exercise a legitimate expression of negative procedural will, i.e., the possibility of withdrawing the urgent protection sought.

BILL NO. 10,128, OF 2018
(From Mr. Bacelar)
Amends the Brazilian Traffic Code, established by Law No. 9,503, of September 23, 1997, to provide
for the substitution of privative of liberty penalty with restrictive of rights penalty for crimes committed
while driving motor vehicles.

DISPACH:
Refer to PL-9823/2018.
CONSIDERATION:
Proposal Subject to Plenary Consideration
THE NATIONAL CONGRESS decrees:

**Article 1**
This Law adds a new §5 to Article 291 of Law No. 9,503, of September 23, 1997, Brazilian Traffic Code, to provide for the substitution of privative imprisonment with restrictive measures for crimes committed while driving motor vehicles.

**Article 2**
Add the following §5 to Article 291 of Law No. 9,503, of September 23, 1997, Brazilian Traffic Code.

"**Article 291.** ..............................................................................
.............................................................................................
§5. The substitution provided for in Article 44, clause I, of Law No. 2,848, of December 7, 1940 (Penal Code), subject to the other conditions set forth in clauses II and III of the aforementioned article's caput, shall only apply in the cases stipulated in Article 302, §3, Article 303, §2, and Articles 308, §§ 1 and 2, all of this Code, provided that a privative imprisonment sentence of not more than five years and six months is applied." (Amended)

**Article 3**
This Law shall enter into force one hundred and twenty days after its official publication.

**Justification**
This proposal aims to prevent the continuation of impunity in traffic situations on Brazilian roads and highways.

Recent legislative changes have seen the National Congress approve increased penalties for drivers who commit crimes while driving motor vehicles under the influence of alcohol and other drugs, as well as during clandestine automobile races, disputes, or competitions.

Law No. 13,546, of 2017, was more than worthy in raising penalties for drivers who, in an irresponsible and reckless manner, put the lives of other drivers and pedestrians at risk, causing losses
May 2018
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES
Tuesday 15 63

Irreparable harm to entire families. Thus, by amending Articles 302, 303, and 308 of the Traffic Code, the aforementioned law increased the provision of privative penalties for the respective criminal types.

However, even though we have harsher penalties for traffic crimes committed under conditions of intoxication, drug use, or clandestine races, criminal legislation, specifically Article 44 of the Penal Code, provides the possibility of substituting privative penalties with restrictive penalties in all these situations.

The modalities of restrictive penalties are: pecuniary compensation; community service or service to public entities; temporary deprivation of rights; and limitation of weekends.

In other words, even if the result of reckless driving is a serious bodily injury or even homicide, regardless of the penalty applied in the specific case, the driver may leave the process without spending even a single day in prison.

We are not against the possibility of substituting penalties in traffic crimes. However, this possibility cannot be considered independently of the penalty applied in the specific case, as provided in the current wording of Article 44, paragraph I, of the Penal Code, for negligent crimes.

We understand that, as in intentional crimes, the possibility of applying the substitution of penalty in traffic crimes committed under the influence of alcohol, drugs, or without authorization, should consider the penalty applied in each case and have a limit.

Therefore, we propose that - in the cases provided in paragraph 3 of Article 302 (homicide while driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs); paragraph 2 of Article 303 (bodily injury while driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs); and paragraphs 1 and 2 of Article 308 (bodily injury and homicide in a race, dispute, or automobile competition without authorization) - the substitution of privative penalties with restrictive penalties is only permitted when the applied penalty is not superior to five years and six months.

Not only in cases of homicide, but also in cases of bodily injury, the driver who consumes alcohol or another intoxicating substance acts recklessly and culpably, assuming the risk of causing traffic accidents with victims. Thus, this bill aims to contribute to a more rigorous and effective legislation that can change the behavior of these drivers.

The sense of impunity, so prevalent in various segments of Brazilian society, cannot prosper, especially when we are talking directly about actions with such high potential for harm. This feeling leads many drivers to disregard the damage they may cause with reckless driving.

This situation needs to be combated.

In light of the above, we request the support of our esteemed colleagues for the approval of this proposal.

Chamber of Sessions, April 25, 2018.

**JUSTIFICATIVA**

The §8th paragraph of Article 57 of Law No. 8.213/91, included by Law No. 9.732 of 11.12.98, states:

§ 8. The provisions of Article 46 shall apply to a retiree, as per this article, who continues to engage in an activity or operation that exposes them to harmful agents as listed in Article 58 of this Law.

Article 57 concerns special retirements for workers exposed to conditions detrimental to health or physical integrity. Article 46, to which the aforementioned clause refers, addresses invalidity retirements:

**Article 46** The retiree by invalidity who voluntarily returns to work shall have their retirement automatically canceled as of the date of return.

Thus, the paragraph to be repealed equates a special, contributory, and scheduled retirement to an invalidity retirement, which is security-based and unpredictable, reserved for those no longer able to work.

However, retirement for workers exposed to harmful conditions is only granted to those who meet all the requirements, such as contribution time and proof of special labor. Once the requirements are met, the insured retires and should be able to decide whether to continue or not in a risky condition. If a special worker, already retired, chooses to remain in the job, already under the guarantee of a social security benefit, they should not be prohibited from doing so. There are several reasons for this:

a) Special retirement is defined by the Federal Constitution (Article 201, §1) and there is no provision for mandatory removal in the article, and ordinary law cannot innovate or restrict a constitutional benefit so significantly.

BILL NO. 10,140, 2018
(From Mr. Patrus Ananias)

DISPACH:

The National Congress decrees:
Art. 1. Article 554 of Law No. 13,105 of March 16, 2015, is amended to add paragraph 4:
Art. 554. ...
§4. In the case of collective possession action, as provided for in §1, no removal may be carried out without ensuring a new, adequate, and dignified dwelling, under penalty of constituting a grave violation of human rights.
Art. 2. This law shall enter into force on the date of its publication.
JUSTIFICATION
The right to dignified housing is a social right constitutionally established in Article 6 of the Federal Constitution, prompting not only the need for a sectoral public policy for social housing but also the obligation to prevent people displaced by various factors from being compulsorily reduced to homelessness.
Furthermore, Brazil has internationally committed to protecting the right to dignified housing at the United Nations Conference on Human Settlements (Habitat). The Conference recommends to countries that they prohibit the legal practice of collective forced evictions, which involves the involuntary transfer of people, families, and groups from their places or communities, exacerbating the housing problem, intensifying conflicts, and aggravating social inequality that is already high in our country.
In Brazil, we daily witness situations such as communities facing reintegration of possession in areas they have occupied for a long time, with all the violence of the state apparatus. The resistance of these people, obviously, stems from the fact that they have no other place to go. The purpose of this bill is to ensure cooperation among all public instances to guarantee that no collective forced removal is carried out before ensuring that the housing right of those families is preserved. In other words, in the preparatory tasks for a collective eviction, there must also be a need to ensure a dignified dwelling for relocation, and only after this verification can a reintegration of possession injunction issued by the Judiciary be carried out without violating the Federal Constitution and International Human Rights Treaties.
Therefore, given the urgency of the approved bill from a humanitarian perspective, we count on the collaboration of our esteemed colleagues to approve it.

BILL NO. 10,142, OF 2018
(From Mr. Glauber Braga)
Amends Law No. 7,210, of July 11, 1984 - Criminal Execution Law - to define guidelines, objectives, and other parameters regarding the work of prisoners in correctional facilities.
DISPOSITION:
ATTACH TO PL-541/2007.
CONSIDERATION:
Proposal Subject to Plenary Consideration
The National Congress decrees:
Article 1. This Law amends the Criminal Execution Law to define guidelines, objectives, and other parameters regarding the work of prisoners in correctional facilities.
Article 2. Law No. 7,210, of July 11, 1984, is amended to read as follows:
“Article 28. ........................................................................................
.....................................................................................................
§ 2. The work of prisoners is subject to the regime of the Consolidation of Labor Laws.
Article 29. The work of prisoners shall be remunerated, based on a prior table, and cannot be below the minimum wage.”
Article 3. This Law enters into force on the date of its publication.
JUSTIFICATION
It is a recognized fact that the Brazilian prison reality is at one of its most severe periods. According to data from the National Penitenciary Information Survey, in June 2016, Brazil had over 726,000 prisoners allocated in just over 368,000 spots, subject to a typical risk of contagion by dermatoses, respiratory diseases, and other epidemics, sleep deprivation, as well as poor nutrition and hydration. Such sufferings are imposed on the bodies of detainees in order to achieve the harmonious social integration of the convicted and guide their return to coexistence in society, as provided by Law 7,210 of 1984, the current Criminal Execution Law, in its Articles 1 and 10. Following the same flawed logic of vulnerability to resocialization and reintegration, the norms regarding the “work of the convicted” are established.
Thus, the Criminal Execution Law establishes in its Articles 28 and 29 that prisoners are not
70 Tuesday 15
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES
May 2018

missing_from_translation: Ação de Descumprimento de Preceito Fundamental

segments.text:
It will have its labor relations subordinate to the CLT and the minimum contraprestation cannot be lower than ¾ of the minimum wage. However, the already mentioned National Penitenciary Information Survey indicates that 75% of prisoners involved in labor activities as of November 2016 received a salary lower than ¾ of the minimum wage or received no salary at all.

Such provisions treat the convicted as inferior and cheaper labor, directly contradicting the 1988 Constitution of the Federative Republic of Brazil, which states in Article 5, caput, that all are equal before the law, without distinction of any kind, and in Article 7, clause IV, that urban and rural workers have the right to a minimum wage, established by law and uniformly applied throughout the nation, sufficient to meet their basic vital needs and those of their families, including housing, food, education, health, leisure, clothing, hygiene, transportation, and social security, with periodic adjustments to preserve their purchasing power, and may not be linked to any other purpose.

Therefore, it can be seen that the current prison structure makes the work allowed to prisoners yet another punitive measure exceeding the individually applied sentences and not provided for in the list of penalties in Article 32 of the Penal Code.

Given the recognition of this unconstitutionality, the Attorney General of the Republic even filed Action of Breach of Fundamental Precept 336 in February 2015 to declare that Article 29, caput, of Law 7.210/84 is not in accordance with the 1988 Federal Constitution, currently awaiting judgment.

In light of the above and to ensure the adherence to a principle already established in the constitution, the support of the noble peers is requested in order to approve this bill.

DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES
Tuesday 15 73

The objective of this legislation is to prevent these products from being irregularly directed to the Brazilian market. To do so, the law requires specific markings on the packaging to identify the products as exports and thus prohibit their destination to Brazil. However, these requirements apply to packaging containing twenty cigarettes, as indicated in the device:

"Article 12. Export cigarettes may not be sold or displayed for sale in the country and must be marked, on the packaging of each pack or folder of 20 (twenty) units, by the equipment referred to in Article 27 of Law No. 11,488, of June 15, 2007, with codes that enable identifying its legitimate origin and preventing the clandestine introduction of these products into the national territory. ..................." (we have emphasized)

Thus, it is implicit that the exportation is limited only to packaging containing twenty cigarettes.

Although the packaging of twenty cigarettes is the standard configuration for the domestic market, the practice of certain foreign markets may differ, for example, packaging containing 18 (United Kingdom), 25 (Australia), or even 40 cigarettes (China), present in some countries. It is therefore noted that the Brazilian legislation imposes a barrier to access to markets that demand packages of different quantities from the national standard.

It is clear that the main objective of the current legal device is not to limit the type of presentation packaging of exported cigarettes, but simply to prohibit the display for sale in Brazil of products destined for abroad and to require that the presentation packaging for the consumer be properly marked to identify its origin. The mention of the pack or folder of twenty cigarettes serves here to delimit the type of packaging to be marked, taking into account the existing standard for Brazil. This is because the same marking relative to the fiscal control of cigarettes destined for the domestic market, which, in fact, is done for packaging containing twenty units, was taken advantage of. However, this delimitation had the undesirable effect of restricting the presentation packaging for the foreign consumer to that of twenty cigarettes, preventing exports to countries that adopt different standards.

It is therefore proposed to amend the legislation to allow cigarettes to be exported in packaging formats different from the Brazilian standard, while maintaining the prohibition against sale in the domestic market and the requirement for marking the presentation packaging for the consumer. Thus, the central measures for combating the diversion or irregular return of these goods to the domestic market are preserved.

Given this, the following proposed text is presented to give a new drafting to the heading of Article 12 of Decree-Law No. 1,593, of 1977:

"Article 12. Export cigarettes may not be sold or displayed for sale in the country and must be marked, on the packaging of each pack, folder, or other presentation format for the consumer, by the equipment referred to in Article 27 of Law No. 11,488, of June 15, 2007, with codes that enable identifying its legitimate origin and preventing the clandestine introduction of these products into the national territory."

These, Mr. President, are the reasons that lead us to propose to Your Excellency the attached draft law.

JUSTIFICATION
Traffic violence in Brazil has reached alarming levels. One person dies on public roads every twelve minutes, and the number of injured is even higher, reaching ten times as many. In an attempt to combat this critical situation, the Brazilian Traffic Code establishes a list of equipment considered mandatory for vehicles circulating in the country, always with a focus on safety. However, we believe that this list can be improved by including two devices that we consider essential to achieve the goal of reducing traffic accident victims.

The first of these devices is the data recorder for vehicle movement - in English, this device is called an Event Data Record (EDR) or simply EDR. Popularly known as the "black box," this equipment is fundamental for forensic activities and traffic accident investigations, as it retrieves important data from the vehicle, such as the speed at the moment of a collision or the identification of any potential mechanical or electronic failure. This facilitates the investigative work, allowing the reconstruction of the event's dynamics and thus establishing the cause of the accident.

In addition to holding culprits accountable, understanding the determining causes and contributing factors of traffic accidents enables traffic managers to adopt prevention programs for future events. Thus, the data extracted from the recording devices will also be used to propose strategies to reduce the alarming accident rates, such as the development of preventive campaigns, driver education, advancements in vehicle and road safety, among others.

The installation of this device is extremely simple, and the increase in the vehicle's selling price will be minimal, as all vehicles equipped with airbags (an already mandatory equipment listed in subparagraph VII of Article 105 of the CTB) already have a control module (on-board computer) that measures the vehicle's deceleration and decides whether it is an accident that requires the activation of the airbag. When the bag is activated, various information can be recorded in the memory of the control module, such as: speed at the moment of impact and in the seconds immediately preceding it, the force of the impact, whether the seatbelt was fastened, whether the brake was applied, whether the anti-lock braking system (ABS) was activated, and even identifying mechanical defects in the vehicle.
86 Tuesday 15
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES
May 2018

In practice, the accident data recorder is no more than a memory space within the airbag module where software collects and records information from various available electronic sensors. The data obtained by the data recorder is very useful for manufacturers themselves for their protection and defense in case of vehicle failure lawsuits, as well as for data collection for product development. In Brazil, some vehicles already have this device, for example, the GM/Onix, the country's best-selling car in 2017.

It is worth remembering that we are in the Decade of Action for Safe Roads (2011-2020), during which governments around the world, including Brazil, commit to taking new measures to prevent and reduce the severity of traffic accidents. Improving the investigation process and subsequent accountability of culprits is one of these measures, both to enhance the effectiveness of punishing traffic infractors and criminals, and to assist in the implementation of preventive actions. Thus, the importance and feasibility of requiring all vehicles to be manufactured with this device are evident. Manufacturers should also make available decoded data in a format that can be read and analyzed by the police authority responsible for investigating the accident.

Another important device to enhance the safety of occupants in school buses and public collective transportation vehicles is that which prevents these vehicles from moving with open doors. Although it may seem absurd, it is not uncommon to see buses and minibuses traveling with open doors, under the pretext of cooling the vehicle's internal temperature and providing greater comfort to users. There are also cases where vehicles move with open doors due to overcrowding. In fact, such situations put the life and physical integrity of passengers at risk. Cases of accidents under these conditions are not rare, especially in urban traffic, including deaths or permanent injuries.

Therefore, the proposal aims to eliminate the possibility of the driver neglecting the safety of passengers, requiring the installation of a device that prevents the vehicle from moving with open doors. However, as current vehicles will not be required to install this device and considering that it can be tampered with later, it will be necessary to provide for an infraction against the driver of a vehicle that travels with open doors, putting passenger safety at risk, reminding that in most cases, this collective transportation is carried out with people standing up, without using the safety belt, which increases the risk of accidents. Since the behavior of traveling with open doors can apply to any vehicle, we are differentiating passenger transportation from school bus transportation, with the latter being more severe.

In light of the above, we request the support of the esteemed Colleagues so that this proposal can be approved and that we can provide greater safety for traffic on Brazilian roads.

This bill aims to simplify certain aspects of drug registration legislation, allowing for faster processes in specific situations, without increasing risk or compromising patient effectiveness.

JUSTIFICATION
The validity period of medications is essential information that must be present on the packaging. Using treatments beyond the validity period may increase the risk of adverse effects and, primarily, reduce effectiveness.

However, studies have questioned the validity periods reported by the industry, suggesting that medications could be used for longer periods than indicated on the packaging.

For example, a study by the University of California analyzed a stock of medications stored for decades, with some exceeding 30-40 years past their validity. The results were surprising: twelve of the fourteen compounds evaluated remained as potent as when they were manufactured1. Another research, conducted in 2006, studied 122 different expired medications, with an average age of over four years. Two-thirds of these remained stable in each test performed.

Addressing this issue has the potential to generate significant savings. The U.S. Department of Defense, in partnership with the FDA, developed a program to manage the validity of its vast stock of medications reserved for disaster situations2. The extension of the validity period led, only in 2016, to a savings of two billion dollars that would have been wasted by destroying still-effective medications.

In Brazil, pharmaceutical manufacturers are currently responsible for informing the permitted use period of medications, but the choice of the deadline does not always follow scientific criteria. The pharmaceutical industry tends to opt for short deadlines to avoid future questions about effectiveness. The early expiration and disposal of medications can result in significant losses.

BILL NO. 10,171, OF 2018
(From Mr. Fábio Trad)
Amends Law No. 2,848, of December 7, 1940 - Penal Code, to establish the crime of illicit enrichment committed by a public official.
DISPOSITION:
ATTACH TO PL-5363/2005.
CONSIDERATION:
Proposal Subject to Plenary Consideration
THE NATIONAL CONGRESS decrees:
Article 1. This Law amends Law No. 2,848, of December 7, 1940 - Penal Code, to establish as a crime of illicit enrichment committed by a public official, when the public official has under his control, possession, and property, in a non-occasional manner, assets, rights, or values whose value is incompatible with his or her earnings obtained due to his or her office, employment, or public function.
Article 2. Add Article 312-A to Law No. 2,848, of December 7, 1940 - Penal Code, as follows:
Illicit Enrichment
Article 312-A. To have under his or her control, possession, or property, in a non-occasional manner, assets, rights, or values whose value is incompatible with his or her earnings obtained due to his or her office, employment, or public function:
Penalty - imprisonment from 4 (four) to 8 (eight) years and a fine.
§ 1. The same penalty applies if there is repayment or extinction of the public official's debts, even by a third party.
§ 2. The penalties are increased by one-half if the ownership or possession of the assets and values is fraudulently attributed to third parties.
Article 3. This Law enters into force on the date of its publication.
JUSTIFICATION
The illicit enrichment of a public official is indirect proof of corruption and related crimes, and particularly in Brazil, it has been reported almost daily by the media. In light of this well-known fact, we propose to present this Bill to consider as a crime under the Penal Code the illicit enrichment of a public official.
Thus, we propose to criminalize having under his or her control, possession, or property, in a non-occasional manner, assets, rights, or values whose value is incompatible with his or her earnings obtained due to his or her office, employment, or public function. Similarly, it is intended to punish with the same penalty if
100 Tuesday 15
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES
May 2018

There is amortization or extinction of public servant debts, or those considered equivalent, including by a third party. To this end, it is proposed to apply the penalty of imprisonment from four to eight years and a fine that can be increased by half if it is proven that the ownership or possession of goods and values is fraudulently attributed to third parties, the so-called "use of 'oranges'".

In this regard, it is important to highlight that the United Nations Convention against Corruption, internalized by Brazil, "exorts States Parties to criminalize in their legal systems the offense of illicit enrichment, defined as a significant increase in the wealth of a public official through income that cannot be reasonably justified by him/her."

In the administrative sphere, the conduct that leads to the characterization of the illicit enrichment of the public agent is provided for in Law No. 8.429/1992, which "provides for the sanctions applicable to public agents in cases of illicit enrichment in the exercise of a mandate, position, employment or function in the direct, indirect or foundation public administration and establishes other provisions," and we can call it another legislative mechanism to combat corruption, particularly in government institutions that inevitably cause damage to the treasury and society.

The presumed illicit enrichment of the public agent occurs when the public agent manifests signs of administrative improbity, a fact resulting from the flagrantly incompatible patrimonial increase with the corresponding remuneration. This is described in Article 9 of Law No. 8.429/92:

"Article 9. Administrative improbity consisting of illicit enrichment is obtained by obtaining any type of patrimonial advantage improperly due to the exercise of a position, mandate, function, employment or activity in the entities mentioned in Article 1 of this law, and particularly:

...

VII. Acquiring, for oneself or for others, in the exercise of a public mandate, position, employment or function, goods of any nature whose value is disproportionate to the evolution of the agent's patrimony or income;"

In its turn, disproportionate assets cannot be considered as evidence of illicit enrichment, unless proven otherwise, although they may give rise to a legal presumption. It is inferred that assets disproportionate to income or the normal patrimonial evolution of a public official, acquired during their term of office, represent the acquisition of an undue advantage due to their office (art. 9 caput) and thus constitute an act of improbity. Of course, a civil servant will always have the possibility to prove the legitimacy of their patrimonial increase, such as an inheritance, a prize, or a lawful activity outside of working hours.

The configuration of this type of administrative act of improbity is subject to penalties such as the loss of public office, suspension of political rights, payment of civil fines, prohibition from contracting with the public sector, etc. (art. 12, item I1), all of which are applicable by the judiciary. In turn, it is up to the administration to apply, based on the Statute of Civil Servants of the Union, the penalty of dismissal (art. 132, item IV).

A practical example of this situation would be a civil servant with a salary of R$5,000.00 (five thousand reais), but whose assets include luxury vessels, properties, and vehicles.

Article 12. Independently of criminal, civil, and administrative penalties provided for in specific legislation, the responsible party for an act of improbity is subject to the following sanctions, which may be applied individually or cumulatively according to the gravity of the fact: I - in the case of art. 9, loss of assets or values illegally added to the patrimony, full reimbursement of any damage, loss of public office, suspension of political rights for eight to ten years, payment of a civil fine of up to three times the value of the illicitly acquired assets, and prohibition from contracting with the public sector or receiving fiscal or credit incentives, directly or indirectly, even through a legal entity in which they are a majority shareholder, for a period of ten years;

Unique Paragraph. In determining the penalties provided for in this law, the judge shall consider the extent of the damage caused, as well as the patrimonial benefit obtained by the agent. (I emphasized)

In terms of luxury, etc. One's wealth will undoubtedly be deemed disproportionate to their income. There is a presumption that the wealth is due to acts of improbity, although they are allowed to prove the legitimate origin of these assets. The legal precept of illicit enrichment as an act of administrative improbity is precisely to allow the punishment of the dishonest servant against whom the original illegal act cannot be pointed out, however, under the penalty of nullity, opportunities will always be given to the servant to clarify the origin of their wealth.

In this context, it is important to highlight that Decree No. 5.483/05, which "regulates, within the Executive Branch, Article 13 of Law 8,429 of June 2, 1992, establishes patrimonial scrutiny and provides for other measures", clarified that the analysis of the public servant's patrimonial evolution can be conducted by the General Control of the Union whenever it deems necessary, and if a patrimonial inconsistency is detected, the investigation procedure should be initiated. Although the percentage falls within the parameters of the World Health Organization (WHO) - of at least 1% of the population - it is still low in terms of blood stock to meet health needs. Indeed, the Ministry of Health has been working to increase the rate. Blood is
May 2018

Irreplaceable. And those who need it can only obtain it through the generosity of those who donate. This Draft Law aims to reinforce the importance of donation, sensitize new volunteers, and retain donors.

The history of hemotherapy in Brazil over the past three decades has recorded significant advancements in the search for a hemotherapy system that provides the population with a final product that is safe and of quality. This was only possible thanks to the restructuring of services, the legitimization of blood donation as a voluntary, altruistic, and unpaid act, as well as technological advancements, legal frameworks, technical norms, capacitations, and modernization of management. DISPOSITION:
TO THE COMMITTEE ON CONSTITUTION, JUSTICE, AND CITIZENSHIP (MERIT AND ART. 54, RICD).
CONSIDERATION:
Proposal Subject to Conclusive Consideration by the Committees - Art. 24 II
THE NATIONAL CONGRESS decrees:
Art. 1 - This Law adds a provision to Law No. 8,935, of November 18, 1994, which
regulates Article 236 of the Federal Constitution, providing for notarial and registration services.
Art. 2 - Law No. 8,935, of November 18, 1994, is amended as follows:
Art. 37-A. Natural or legal persons designated by the competent organs of the states and the Federal District, in accordance with state and district legislation, to manage the collection and transfers of resources intended for the compensation of free civil registration acts of natural persons and for the complementation of the minimum revenue of deficitary offices, as well as those responsible for resources intended for the pension funds of registrars and notaries, have the duty to account, as public resource managers, and must document all corresponding acts, as well as submit them to oversight, presenting a detailed documentary report to the respective courts of justice and accounting boards on a semi-annual basis.
§ 1 - The duty to account provided for in the preceding paragraph is independent of any additional regulation in place for its implementation, even if operational rules are established within the competence of the oversight bodies.
Art. 3 - This Law enters into force on the date of its publication.
JUSTIFICATION
Law No. 8.935/94, which provides for notarial and registration services, should also aim to ensure transparency and integrity in the management of public resources. Despite the obligation of any public resource manager to account, since the enactment of the aforementioned norm, as well as subsequent ones on fees, there is a gap to be addressed, either because it would not be justified in the light of public law imperatives, or due to the need to adapt this normative instrument to the current reality and the society's expectations, making this duty clear and unquestionable.
Thus, in compliance with other relevant regulations on the subject and, seeking to fill the aforementioned gap in the best way possible, it was deemed necessary to insert the normative provision in question so that both resources intended for the compensation of registrars related to free acts practiced and the complementation of the minimum revenue of deficitary offices, as well as those intended for the pension fund of registrars and notaries, while public resources, are clearly and formally submitted to oversight.
May 2018
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES
Tuesday 15 107

To the competent Justice Courts (as already provided for other cases in Article 37 and following of the same Law No. 8.935/94), and to the review of the respective Audit Courts, fulfilling their "end mission" of oversight.

Currently, there is no specific determination regarding the management, allocation, and oversight of these resources, nor is there an obligation to submit them to the competent bodies. In the absence of explicit legal provisions, we have supplied them with this Draft Law.

The Federal Constitution, in particular Article 71, subparagraph II, in conjunction with Article 75, entrusts these Courts with the oversight of "accounting, financial, budgetary, operational, and patrimonial" matters, as well as the judgment of accounts of any individuals responsible for public funds, goods, and values, as in the case at hand.

Indeed, considering that our legislation must be in harmony with the Magna Carta and that, when it comes to public resources, there are no exceptions that allow for any non-compliance with the proposed directives, it becomes imperative to include this legal command, which, in fact, is not innovative but merely aligns with the Major Norm as it should have been this way long ago.

(From Mr. Felipe Bornier)
Adds article 69-A to Law No. 13,146, of July 6, 2015 (Statute of the Person with Disabilities), to make mandatory in commercial establishments the availability of accessible card processing terminals for individuals with visual impairments.
DISPOSITION:
ATTACH TO PL-2285/2015.
CONSIDERATION:
Proposition Subject to Plenary Consideration
THE NATIONAL CONGRESS decrees:
Article 1. This law makes mandatory in commercial establishments that accept debit or credit cards as a means of payment, the availability of accessible card processing terminals for individuals with visual impairments.
Article 2. Law No. 13,146, of July 6, 2015, is amended by adding the following article 69-A:
“Article 69-A
Payment acquirers must ensure the availability of

accessible processing terminals for people with visual impairments.
§ 1. Commercial establishments that accept debit or credit cards as
payment instruments are obligated to maintain at least one processing terminal
as provided in the heading.
§ 2. For the purposes of this article, the following are considered:
I – accessible, a processing terminal that, without compromising the privacy of
the consumer, allows for tactile or auditory reading of the payment-related
information;
II – payment acquirer, the legal entity that facilitates purchase and sale
services and resource movement through transactions with debit and credit cards,
within a payment arrangement, as defined by the Central Bank of Brazil.
(AMENDMENT)
Art. 3º O The Executive Branch shall regulate the provisions of this Law within one hundred and eighty days of its publication.
Art. 4. This Law enters into force one hundred and eighty days after its publication.
May 2018
DIARY OF THE HOUSE OF DEPUTIES
Tuesday 15 111

**Justification**

The modernization of consumer relations has driven diversification not only in the way products and services are offered but also in the expansion of payment instruments, particularly in retail trade.

The use of debit and credit cards has moved beyond mere convenience to become a reality in the daily routines of many consumers, who choose this technology for various reasons: security, convenience, speed of transactions, obtaining advantages, expense control, among others.

For individuals with visual impairments, "plastic money" (as credit or debit cards are known) serves as an accessibility tool, as it allows autonomy in payment operations and avoids carrying and constantly handling large amounts of paper currency, which poses security risks.

However, despite the technological dynamism of so-called "terminals" that process payments made with cards, product and service providers have not made available models that effectively meet the needs of this consumer public.

A notice released in 2015 by the National Organization of the Blind in Brazil - ONCB1 criticizes this disparity. It highlights that "the traditional models of machines for credit and debit card payments, which had tactile relief signage for the number 5 and main keys, are rapidly being replaced by debit card machines with touch screens."

It also emphasizes that, "due to their flawed and restrictive design, these machines deprive individuals with visual impairments of the use of touch, subjecting them to significant embarrassment during financial transactions, such as repeatedly trying to enter a PIN until it is blocked, having to pass their card PIN to a known person to enter it, or more seriously, if they are unaccompanied, having to disclose their PIN to a stranger to enter it."

There are also reports that certain establishments force individuals with visual impairments to use their personal mobile phones as payment terminals, or offer optical character recognition (OCR or QR code) technology that, similarly, is not a suitable solution for this consumer public's access to payment information.

Beyond any doubt, these situations are unimaginable in the current stage of accessibility discipline, whose efforts are directed towards promoting and guaranteeing social inclusion and the exercise of rights.

This proposal aims to inform the consumer, in an easily accessible location on the electronic site page used in e-commerce, about the customer service (SAC) telephone number.
This relevant information about the SAC telephone number, which relates to the offer, presentation, and advertising, particularly in the context of e-commerce on the internet, although already well established in the discipline of our Consumer Protection and Defense Code (CDC), requires better regulation in federal legislation.
Although there is already regulation on the matter at the sub-legal level, namely Decree No. 7,962, of 2013, which "regulates Law No. 8,078, of September 11, 1990, to provide for contracting in e-commerce", we consider that the norm contained in its Article 21 is not sufficient to curb the frequent abuses committed by various e-commerce sites operating in Brazil.
The fact is that the absence of SAC telephone information persists, and virtual stores, with the following provision:
"Articles The electronic sites or other electronic means used for the offer or conclusion of a consumer contract shall make available, in a prominent and easily visible location, the following information:
I - Business name and supplier's registration number, if any, in the National Register of Natural Persons or in the National Register of Legal Entities of the Ministry of Finance;
II - Physical and electronic address, and other necessary information for its location and contact;” (I have emphasized)

The consent of the deficient oversight and enforcement of the institutions comprising the National System for Consumer Defense has been exploited of this weakness in regulation to continue prejudicing the consumer's access to a service that provides them with security and promptness during their purchase of goods and services in the virtual environment of e-commerce.

In fact, although the Consumer Defense Code (CDC) is an extremely effective and successful law, it was enacted (1990) when the internet was not yet an inseparable part of people's lives and did not hold the importance it does today in the percentage of product and service negotiations. As a predominantly principled instrument, it still provides the means to address consumer defense in any contracting medium. However, there are specificities in e-commerce that can be more effectively disciplined. Therefore, it is appropriate to reflect on ways to enhance consumer safeguards in the virtual environment. Much progress has already been made in this regard.

To this end, we propose the mandatory provision that will undoubtedly bring even greater security to the Brazilian consumer during their use of online stores, as they will always be able to rely on the important assistance of the Consumer Service (SAC). We are evolving rapidly in terms of Internet trade, but this evolution cannot surpass consumer protection. Today, the Brazilian consumer who needs to resolve a negative issue such as delayed deliveries, package loss, damaged or exchanged products, is limited to one form of service, which is mostly flawed and inconsistent.

Over the years, it would come to rely on what the current law on parental alienation (Law No. 12.318 of August 26, 2010) stipulates to actually obtain a change in custody of the child to a shared custody arrangement or its reversal in favor of the father.

In genuine situations, it will be observed, as a result of this behavior and the measures then taken by the judiciary, a complete perversion of the law capable of also enabling the repetition of sexual abuse or crimes against children and adolescents by the parent who has previously committed them, with serious risks of severe harm arising for the physical, sexual and/or psychological integrity and the regular physical and mental development of the victims.

Therefore, it is urgent to adopt legislative measures to improve the current law on parental alienation so that situations like these are avoided.

With these proposed amendments, we believe that the occurrence of situations like those reported in the mentioned television program will be, to some extent, hindered without, however, distorting the current law on parental alienation to remove its desired effectiveness in other cases where this legal document already serves an important function in protecting children and adolescents and their families.
